en: The Minor Exposition:
The Exposition of the Pārāyana Chapter:
The Exposition of the Questions.
12. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Bhadrāvudha "Abandoning the attachment to home, cutting off craving,
and unshakable," (so said the Venerable Bhadrāvudha).
Having heard of the Naga who has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, is liberated,
and has cast off the cycle of time— the wise one— I entreat him; they shall turn away from here.
"Abandoning the abode, cutting off craving, and unshakable.

"Abandoning the abode" means that whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, clinging, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding the form element—these have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered incapable of further growth.
They are rendered non-existent and subject to the law of non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha has abandoned his dwelling-place.
[The same applies to] the element of feeling ... pe ... [the other elements].

Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and grasping, whatever mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are in regard to the element of perception … the element of volitional formations … the element of consciousness, [these are suffering].
These have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha has abandoned the home;
he is the cutter of craving.
"Craving" refers to craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
That craving has been cut off, severed, completely eradicated, stilled, and calmed by the Buddha, the Blessed One; it is incapable of arising again, having been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddha is "one who has cut off craving."
“O Wanderer, ‘wandering’ refers to craving.
That which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness—that wandering, that craving, has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One;
it has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.”
Therefore, the Buddha is unshaken.
Because he has abandoned shaking, the Blessed One does not waver in gain, nor does he waver in loss; he does not waver in fame, nor does he waver in disrepute;
he does not waver in praise, nor does he waver in blame; he does not waver even in pleasure.
"Even in suffering, he does not waver, does not shake, does not tremble, does not quiver, does not quake. Therefore, the Buddha is "unshakable"—
the one who has abandoned the home, who cuts off craving, and is unshakable.
"Thus the Venerable Bhadrāvudha.
*Iti* is a grammatical euphonic junction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...
*Āyasmā* is a term of endearment (*piyavacana*)... [etc. ...
"Bhadrāvudha" is the name of that brahmin... [as before] ...the expression—"thus spoke the Venerable Bhadrāvudha.
"The one who has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, and is liberated"—here "delight" (nandī) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, and root of unwholesomeness there may be—that delight is craving.
That has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
Therefore, the Buddha is the "one who has abandoned delight."

"Crossed over the flood," said the Blessed One, "is one who has crossed over the flood of sensual desire, crossed over the flood of existence, crossed over the flood of views, crossed over the flood of ignorance, crossed over the entire path of saṃsāra; one who has emerged, crossed beyond, transcended, fully transcended, and passed beyond it.

He has completed his residence [in the training], fulfilled his practice... for him there is no further becoming in the cycle of birth and death—he is the abandoner of delight who has crossed over the flood."
"Liberated" means that the Blessed One’s mind is freed, liberated, well-liberated from lust; his mind is [freed] from hatred... from delusion...
down to... his mind is freed, liberated, well-liberated from all unwholesome volitional formations—thus he has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, and is liberated.
"Sumedha, entreat the Abandoner of the World-age.
"World-age" (kappa) refers to two world-ages:
the world-age of craving and the world-age of views... [and so forth].
This is the construction of craving... [and so on] ...this is the construction of views.
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished.
Because of the abandoning of the fabrication of craving and because of the relinquishing of the fabrication of views, he is therefore called the Buddha who has abandoned fabrication.
"I entreat" means: I entreat, I beseech, I request, I accept [the offer], I aspire, I long for, I pray, I yearn intensely.
"Sumedhā" (the wise one) is said to be wisdom (*paññā*).
That which is wisdom, understanding ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
The Blessed One is endowed with this intelligence and wisdom, fully endowed, arrived at, fully arrived at, possessed of, fully possessed of, equipped with.
Therefore, the Buddha is "the one of excellent wisdom."
"I implore the wise one for an eon.
Having heard the Naga, they will turn away from here.
"Of the Naga" means [he is] a Naga.

The Blessed One does not come, thus he is a *nāga*; he does not go, thus he is a *nāga*; he does not arrive, thus he is a *nāga* ... [and so on] ... in this way, the Blessed One does not go, thus he is a *nāga*.

Having heard the speech, the expression, the teaching, the instruction, and the admonition of the *nāga*, they will turn away from here—having heard, listened to, mastered, retained, and discerned it.
"Having heard that they will depart, they will set out, and they will go to the cardinal and intermediate directions,
they will turn away from here"— having heard this from the Naga,
the brahmin spoke thus.
“Abandoning the home, cutting off craving, unshakable—
(Thus spoke the Venerable Bhadrāvudha)—
Abandoning delight, having crossed the flood, liberated.”
“Having heard the Naga, people from various regions will turn away from here and entreat the wise one, the abandoner of the world-age.
Thus, people gathered from various districts—
O Hero, desiring your word,
please explain this to them well,
for this Dhamma is known to you.
"Various people gathered from various countries.
"Various people" refers to kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans.
"Gathered from various countries" refers to those from Aṅga, Magadha, Kaliṅga, Kāśī, Kosala, and Vajjī.
The Mallas, the Cetis, the Vamsas, the Kurus, the Pañcālas, the Macchas, the Surasenas, the Assakas,
the Avantīs, the Yonas, and the Kambojas.
"Assembled" means gathered together, come together, united, and met.
People from various regions have gathered together,
longing for your words, O Hero. "Hero" (vīra) means one who is brave.
The Blessed One is a hero because he possesses energy; he is a hero because he is abundant; he is a hero because he has conquered the poison; he is a hero because he is self-sufficient;
and he is a hero because his hair has stood on end [in awe]. Having desisted here from all evils, the one who dwells in energy has transcended the suffering of hell.
"Thus one who possesses energy and exerts effort, such a hero is called 'one who is thus' (tathatta).
"O Hero, longing for your word" means: your speech, your manner of expression, your teaching, your instruction, and that which has been taught.
"Longing for"— meaning longing, desiring, approving, aspiring, yearning, and craving—
longing for your word, O Hero. "To them,
please explain well."
"Of them" means of those khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans.
"You" refers to the Blessed One.
"Please explain" means: please declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make manifest.
Please explain this well to them;
for indeed this Dhamma has been known by you— indeed this Dhamma has been known, weighed, deliberated upon, clarified, and fully manifested by you—
thus indeed has this Dhamma been known by you.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“People of various kinds have gathered from the countryside,
O Hero, longing for your word.”
Please explain this well to them,
for this Dhamma is known to you. One should eliminate all craving for grasping.
(Bhadrāvudha, the Blessed One said:
"Above, below, across, and also in the middle—
whatever in the world they cling to,"
For that very reason, Māra follows after a person.
"One should subdue all craving for grasping"—here, "craving for grasping" refers to craving for form... [and so on]. For what reason is it called "craving for grasping"?
Because it is the cause of grasping. Therefore, it is called "craving for grasping."
Through that craving, they take up, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere to form;
[they do the same with] feeling … perception … [and so on].
Volitional formations … consciousness … destiny …
rebirth … relinking … existence …
They take up, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere to saṃsāra— the round of existence.
For that reason, it is called "craving for grasping."

"One should subdue all craving for grasping" means: one should subdue, thoroughly subdue, abandon, dispel, bring to an end, and lead to the non-existence of all craving for grasping—thus, "one should subdue all craving for grasping.
"O Bhadrāvudha," said the Blessed One.
"Bhadrāvudha," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for veneration... [as before] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely "Blessed One"—thus, "Bhadrāvudha, Blessed One."
"Above, below, across, and in the middle":
"above" refers to the future;
"below" refers to the past.
"Across and in the middle" refers to the present.
"Above" refers to the world of the devas;
"below" refers to the world of hell.
And "across" refers to the human world.
Alternatively, "above" refers to wholesome states;
"below" refers to unwholesome states.
And "across" and "in the middle" refer to indeterminate phenomena (*avyākata-dhamma*).
"Above" refers to the formless realm (*arūpa-dhātu*);
"below" refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
"Across and in the middle" refers to the form element (*rūpadhātu*).
"Above" refers to pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*);
"below" refers to painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*).
"Across and in the middle" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Above" means above the soles of the feet;
"below" means below the crown of the head.
"Across and in the middle" means:
above, below, across, and in the middle.
"Whatever in the world they cling to" means whatever has come to be form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, that they take up, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere to.
"In the world" means in the world of the states of misery … [etc.

… in the world of the sense bases—whatever one clings to in the world, Māra follows that very person because of that very formative activity of karma; thus, "Māra of the aggregates" refers to the rebirth-linking aggregates.
The Mara of the elements, the Mara of the sense-bases, the Mara of the destiny, the Mara of rebirth, the Mara of re-linking, the Mara of existence, the Mara of saṃsāra,
and the Mara of the round follow, pursue, and track him down.
"Jantu" refers to a being, a person, a human, a youth, a man, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a sentient being, a mortal, and a human.
For that very reason, Māra follows after a person.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"One should subdue all craving for grasping."
(Bhadrāvudha, the Blessed One said:
"Above, below, across, and also in the middle—
whatever in the world they cling to,"
“By that very [craving], Māra follows after a person.
Therefore, a wise bhikkhu, being mindful, should not cling to anything in the entire world.
Beholding this generation clinging to the realm of death as if it were a grasping being,
therefore, one who understands should not cling.
Therefore—for that reason, for that cause, for that condition, for that source—seeing this danger in the craving for grasping, it is said "therefore.
One who knows, one who understands, one who comprehends, one who discerns, one who penetrates, one who pierces through, understands: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" ... [and so on] ...
"Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease"—knowing this, understanding it, comprehending it, discerning it, penetrating it, and piercing through it.

"One would not cling" means one would not take up form, would not cling to it, would not grasp it, would not misapprehend it, and would not adhere to it; [and likewise] feeling... [etc.]... [one would not cling].
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
destiny … rebirth … re-linking …
"One would not take up existence… saṃsāra… the round, would not cling to it, would not grasp it, would not misapprehend it, and would not adhere to it"— thus.
Therefore, one who understands should not cling.
"A mindful bhikkhu [should abandon] all acquisitions in the world.
Here, "bhikkhu" refers either to a bhikkhu who is a virtuous ordinary person (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) or to a bhikkhu who is a trainee (*sekkha*).
"He is mindful" by reason of four causes:
when he develops the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, he is mindful ... [and so on] ...
thus he is called "mindful."
The mindful bhikkhu:
"Possession" (*kiñcana*) refers to anything belonging to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"In the entire world" (*sabbaloke*) means in the entire world of the lower realms, the entire world of humans, the entire world of devas, the entire world of aggregates, the entire world of elements, and the entire world of sense bases.
“A mindful bhikkhu [should see] nothing as a possession in the entire world.
Regarding the phrase “beholding beings who grasp”: those who take up, cling to, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to form are called “beings who grasp”;
[those who do so with] feeling … [and so on].
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
… destiny … rebirth … reconnection …
They take up existence... they take up the round of rebirth... they take up the cycle; they grasp it, cling to it, and adhere to it.
*Itīti*: this is a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*)...

[and so on] ...this "iti" refers to the sequential order of the words. *Pekkhamāno*: looking, seeing, being seen, perceiving, beholding, surveying, contemplating, examining—one who looks upon living beings as they grasp [at existence].
"This generation is clinging in the realm of death. "Generation" (*pajā*) is a designation for sentient beings.
By "the realm of death," the defilements (*kilesa*), the aggregates (*khandha*), and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) are meant.
This generation—sentient beings—is clinging, attached, stuck, fastened, and obstructed within the realm of death, the realm of Māra, the realm of mortality.
Just as a commodity might be stuck, entangled, adhered to, clinging, attached,
or obstructed on a wall-plate or a peg, even so, in the realm of death, the realm of Māra, the realm of mortality, beings are stuck, entangled, adhered to, clinging, attached, and obstructed.
This generation is clinging within the realm of death.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Therefore, knowing this, one should not cling.”
The bhikkhu, mindful, sees no possession in the whole world;
beholding these beings as grasping creatures,
he sees this generation clinging within the realm of death.
With the conclusion of the verse... [as before] ...
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This is the twelfth exposition: The Question of the Young Brahmin Bhadrāvudha.
